translation: The pattern of external contraction of the cold pathogen, the ailment of physical form from loss of regulation in food and drink and toil, and internal injury of food and drink all have cold and heat. All the world takes the disease of insufficiency from internal injury of food and drink, loss of regulation, and toil and treats it as the external contraction of the cold pathogen with excess and repletion in the surface, and instead drains its surface. Are the deaths from this wrongness countable? They all arise from not distinguishing its cold and heat. Now let me minutely decompose it. In external contraction of the cold pathogen, [there is] heat [with] aversion to cold, and cold and heat appear together. Its heat, [being] "翕翕" fluttering heat, is also called "拂拂" — heat that arises upon the skin and hair, like the brushing of a feather. This makes clear that its heat is in the surface; it is the cold pathogen invading the very tops of high [levels]. The skin, hair, and interstices are the yang portion, the portion nourished by the Original Qi of the defensive [qi]. Being seized by the cold pathogen, the yang portion is constricted and suppressed, the yang cannot stretch forth, and therefore [there is] fever. Its face is red, the nasal qi is obstructed and not clear, and within the heart [there is] vexation and oppression. Slightly exposing the skin of the body, [the patient] is already unable to endure its cold. Its superficial vacuous heat is only this and nothing more. As to its aversion to cold, even with heavy clothing, covered under curtains, or drawn near to a blazing fire, [the patient] can in the end not resist its cold. Moment by moment and day by day it increases and becomes more severe; only after it must transmit into the interior and form the lower [bowel] pattern does it cease. Its cold and heat appear together, without any interruption. As to internal injury of food and drink, or injury from toil, there is also headache, stiff nape, and lumbar pain, in slight similarity to the taiyang surface pattern; the rest are all different, and [I] have differentiated this in the discourse. In disease of insufficiency from internal injury, there is no yang on the surface, and [the patient] cannot withstand wind and cold; this occurs constantly. Its restless heat arising between the kidneys occurs only occasionally. This is in no way similar to externally contracted cold pathogen. Its aversion to wind and cold arises because the nutritive qi, from insufficiency of the spleen and stomach, flows downward and seizes the kidney and liver — this is the bud of wilting, reversal, and uprushing qi. If the stomach qi were normal, when food and drink enter the stomach, its nutritive qi ascends to spread over the heart and lung, to nourish the skin of the upper burner and the Original Qi of the interstices. Since it already flows downward, the heart and lung have nothing received; there is no yang between the skin; [the patient] loses the outer guard of the Nutritive and Defensive [qi]; hence the yang portion, between skin and body hair, becomes weak and vacuous. Only when [the patient] sees wind or cold, or when dwelling in a yin-cold place or in a place without sunlight, does he hate it. This is constant, without interruption. But when [the patient] avoids wind and cold and keeps to warm places, or adds clothing and covers to warm and nourish his skin, the hated wind and cold then no longer appear. As for this heat — it is not heat from surface contraction of cold pathogen arising between skin and body hair, but rather the damp qi that the kidney receives from the downward flow of the spleen and stomach, which blocks its lower part and causes the yin fire to gush upward, producing steaming restless heat that reaches up through the crown of the head, spreads sideways through the skin and hair, and generates steaming restless heat over the whole body. Only when [the patient] removes clothing and exposes himself, or approaches a cool place, does it cease; or when heat reaches its extreme and sweat issues, it also resolves. As for that external damage's aversion to cold and fever — does it ever produce sweat? If [the patient] obtains sweat then the disease is cured. Using this to differentiate, is it not as easy to see as black and white? When [a person] is injured because his interior is vacuous, [there is] restless heat. Or because wind-cold qi is drawn in through the mouth, suppressing its yin fire and causing the pharynx and diaphragm to be obstructed; the drawn-in qi, wishing to enter, is repelled by the fire of the Chong vessel above the diaphragm, causing the yin qi not to enter; the qi within the chest is suppressed by external wind-cold and cannot stretch forth, causing the mouth to open and the eyes to stare; in the extreme, the voice issues externally, and the qi cannot go up or down, blocked in the throat, and the qi is about to be severed. Or again because of hiccup, because of vomiting, the restless heat arises and must have a cause in order for this pattern to appear. Then the surface vacuity's pattern of aversion to wind and cold again appears. The weakness of the vacuous surface, being seized by the yin fire, [and] restless heat arises but passes in an instant; then the surface vacuity without yang, unable to withstand wind and cold, again appears. This surface vacuity without yang is constant; its restless heat occurs only occasionally. These two are not together: when restless, the cold has ceased; when cold, the restless has ceased — not like the cold and heat of external injury that appear together without interruption. All the hundred diseases have body heat, also called muscular heat, also called heat between skin and body. It is that which one only knows by feeling it with the hand. This is the fever of the body that has form and substance. It too must await the harmonization of yin and yang, and it resolves when sweat issues. One must be careful not to use this to differentiate, because vacuity and repletion, internal and external diseases all have it, and so it is hard to differentiate. Only following this explanation — [using] the heat that the patient himself feels as fever and aversion to cold, and the heat of the restless attacks — as the standard [in differentiation] is the criterion.
